question: What is the fundamental difference between TCP and UDP?

options.text: TCP and UDP operate at different layers of the TCP/IP model
options.explanation: Both protocols operate at the transport layer of the TCP/IP model

options.text: TCP guarantees delivery and packet order, UDP does not
options.explanation: TCP uses acknowledgment (ACK), retransmission, and packet numbering mechanisms to guarantee reliable delivery

options.text: UDP cannot transmit data over a network
options.explanation: UDP fully transmits data, just without delivery guarantees. It is widely used for video calls, gaming, and DNS queries

options.text: TCP is faster than UDP
options.explanation: The opposite is true: UDP is faster because it doesn't spend time on handshake, acknowledgments, and order control

question: What problem does HTTP/2 multiplexing solve compared to HTTP/1.1?

options.text: Completely eliminates all types of HOL blocking
options.explanation: HTTP/2 eliminates HTTP-level HOL blocking, but TCP-level HOL blocking remains: a lost TCP packet blocks all streams. This is only solved in HTTP/3 (QUIC)

options.text: Reduces transmitted data size through binary request body format
options.explanation: HTTP/2 uses binary framing for headers (HPACK), but the request body is sent as-is. Multiplexing is about parallel streams, not compression

options.text: Enables encryption (TLS)
options.explanation: TLS is available in HTTP/1.1 too (HTTPS). Multiplexing is unrelated to encryption

options.text: HTTP-level Head-of-Line blocking — requests no longer wait in queue
options.explanation: HTTP/2 allows sending many requests in parallel within a single TCP connection via streams, eliminating the queue at the HTTP level

question: How is a WebSocket connection established?

options.text: Client sends a UDP packet to initialize WebSocket
options.explanation: WebSocket runs over TCP, not UDP. It starts with an HTTP request and then switches protocol

options.text: Client opens a separate TCP connection on a special WebSocket port
options.explanation: WebSocket uses the same ports as HTTP (80/443). The connection is established via HTTP Upgrade, not a separate port

options.text: Server initiates the connection to the client
options.explanation: The client always initiates. The server cannot open a WebSocket connection to a client — it only accepts and confirms the upgrade request

options.text: Via HTTP Upgrade handshake: client sends an HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket header
options.explanation: WebSocket starts as a regular HTTP request. The server responds with 101 Switching Protocols, and the connection switches to full-duplex mode

question: What advantages does gRPC gain from using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers?

options.text: Native browser support without additional proxies
options.explanation: Browsers don't support gRPC directly due to browser HTTP/2 API limitations. A grpc-web proxy (e.g., Envoy) is needed

options.text: Multiplexing — many RPC calls through a single TCP connection
options.explanation: HTTP/2 allows gRPC to send many RPC calls in parallel via streams within a single connection

options.text: Bidirectional streaming — client and server can simultaneously send data streams
options.explanation: HTTP/2 streams allow gRPC to implement four communication modes, including bidirectional streaming

options.text: Binary serialization — payload 3-10x smaller than JSON
options.explanation: Protocol Buffers encode data into a compact binary format, significantly saving bandwidth compared to text-based JSON

question: You typed https://shop.example.com in your browser. In what order do network operations occur?

options.text: HTTP request → DNS lookup → TLS handshake → TCP handshake
options.explanation: The HTTP request is sent last, after you already have the IP (DNS), TCP connection, and encrypted channel (TLS)

options.text: DNS lookup → TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request
options.explanation: First you need the IP address (DNS), then establish a TCP connection (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK), then set up an encrypted channel (TLS), and only then send the HTTP request

options.text: TLS handshake → TCP handshake → DNS lookup → HTTP request
options.explanation: TLS runs over TCP, so TCP is needed first. And TCP is impossible without an IP, which DNS provides

options.text: TCP handshake → DNS lookup → HTTP request → TLS handshake
options.explanation: You can't establish a TCP connection without knowing the server's IP address. DNS lookup is always the first step
